procedural_history.originating_court: High Court for the State of Telangana at Hyderabad
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 18 April 2023 of a single Judge of the High Court in Criminal Petition No 3798 of 2023. The High Court (i) granted an ad interim stay of arrest to the first respondent; and (ii) directed that the examination before the CBI in the course of the investigation shall be “in printed/written form” during the course of which a questionnaire may also be handed over to the first respondent.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The first respondent filed a Writ Petition (CRLP No. 3798 of 2023) before the High Court seeking anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 in connection with RC-04(S)/2020/SC-III/ND. On 10 March 2023, the High Court directed the CBI to produce the entire record and not to take any coercive steps against the first respondent, while ordering him to appear before the Investigating Officer on 14 March 2023. On 13 March 2023, the High Court reserved orders. On 17 March 2023, the High Court disposed of IA Nos 1 and 2 in the Writ Petition holding that it was not inclined to stay the examination of the first respondent under Section 161 of the CrPC. While vacating the interim order, the High Court, however, directed that the first respondent shall be examined within the sight of his advocate.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (daughter of the deceased) appealed the High Court's order to the Supreme Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1251 of 2023. The appellant and her mother had also previously moved the Supreme Court seeking transfer of the trial and a direction to the CBI to conclude the investigation in a time bound manner, apprehending danger to witnesses and false complaints against CBI officers. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned order of the High Court, finding that the High Court's directions regarding the form of the investigation would stultify the investigation and were inappropriate.

directions: The impugned order of the High Court dated 18 April 2023 is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting an ad interim stay of arrest.

facts: The first respondent, a suspect in a murder investigation, was summoned by the CBI.
The respondent applied for anticipatory bail in the High Court.
While the bail application was still pending, the High Court passed an ad interim order on April 18, 2023.
This interim order stayed the respondent's arrest and directed that the CBI's examination of the respondent be conducted in a "printed/written form," potentially with a questionnaire.
application: The Supreme Court found the High Court's order to be "extraordinary" and premature, as the main anticipatory bail application had not yet been decided.
The Court held that there was "absolutely no warrant" for the High Court to direct the investigation to be conducted in writing.
It also found it "wholly inappropriate" for the High Court to suggest that a questionnaire be handed over to the respondent.
The Supreme Court reasoned that such directions would "stultify the investigation" and "gravely prejudice" its course.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in granting the ad interim stay of arrest with the attached conditions. It found that the High Court had misapplied itself by passing an order that improperly interfered with the investigation process. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in directing that the examination before the CBI in the course of the investigation shall be in printed/written form during the course of which a questionnaire may also be handed over to the first respondent.

facts: The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) was investigating a murder and had issued summons to the first respondent for questioning.
The first respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court.

The High Court, in an order dated April 18, 2023, directed that the first respondent's examination by the CBI should be conducted in a "printed/written form" and that a questionnaire could be handed over to him.
The High Court also granted an ad interim stay on the respondent's arrest.
law: The judiciary should not interfere with the process of a criminal investigation in a manner that hampers or prejudices its course.

The method and manner of interrogation are matters for the investigating agency to determine, and it is inappropriate for a court to prescribe specific procedures like written questioning or providing a questionnaire in advance.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's directions were "extraordinary" and "unwarranted."
It reasoned that forcing the CBI to conduct the examination in a "printed or written form" and to provide a questionnaire would "stultify the investigation."

The Court held that such an order was "wholly inappropriate" and would "gravely prejudice the course of investigation," particularly when the CBI was still in the process of investigating the crime and the roles of various suspects.
The Supreme Court also noted that the High Court's order was "premature," especially in light of the information the CBI had presented in its affidavit.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's directive, concluding that there was "absolutely no warrant" for a court to dictate the method of interrogation. It held that the order would severely hamper the investigation and was an improper judicial intervention. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the impugned order of the High Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court, when considering an application for an ad-interim stay of arrest pending the final disposal of an anticipatory bail application, should not make substantive observations on the merits of the main application.
obiter: The observations made by a higher court in its order shall not influence the lower court's evaluation of a pending application for anticipatory bail.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's directions, specifically the ad interim stay of arrest and the mandate for a written/printed examination with a questionnaire, were entirely unwarranted and would stultify the criminal investigation. The Court found such orders to be wholly inappropriate, especially at a stage where the CBI was still investigating the broader conspiracy and the roles of multiple accused, and determined that these directions were liable to gravely prejudice the course of the investigation.
legal_tests_applied: The court did not apply a specific named legal test but reasoned based on the general principle that judicial orders should not unduly interfere with or prejudice an ongoing criminal investigation, particularly at a preliminary stage.
policy_considerations: The court's decision was driven by the policy of ensuring that the course of a criminal investigation is not gravely prejudiced by judicial intervention. It emphasized that allowing an investigating agency, in this case the CBI, to fully investigate a crime and the roles of all potential accused without being hampered by inappropriate procedural constraints (like written questionnaires) is critical for the integrity of the justice system. The court stated, "Particularly at this stage when the CBI is to fully investigate the crime and the role of several accused who do not form a part of the charge sheet as submitted, we are of the view that the directions issued by the High Court were unwarranted."
